content: The World Health Organization (WHO) in 2015 recommended atovaquone-proguanil as a treatment option for travelers and as an alternative therapy in malaria-endemic regions when first-line artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) is unavailable or ineffective. It can also be used in combination with artesunate. This review updates a Cochrane Review from 2005 and evaluates the efficacy and safety of atovaquone-proguanil, both alone and in combination with artemisinin drugs, compared to other antimalarial treatments for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in adults and children. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that reported efficacy and safety data for atovaquone-proguanil or its combination with a partner drug, compared to at least one other antimalarial drug. The search for trials was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, with the last search performed on January 30, 2020. Seventeen RCTs involving 4763 participants from Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia met the inclusion criteria. Eight trials provided polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-adjusted data to differentiate between new infections and recrudescent infections during follow-up. The review focused on comparisons with three WHO-recommended antimalarial regimens. 1. Comparison with Artemether-Lumefantrine: In a 2008 trial from Ethiopia with 60 participants, there were two PCR-adjusted treatment failures at day 28 in the atovaquone-proguanil group, compared to none in the artemether-lumefantrine group. In a 2012 trial from Colombia with 208 participants, there was one PCR-adjusted treatment failure in each group at day 42. 2. Comparison with Artesunate-Amodiaquine: A 2014 trial in Cameroon reported six PCR-adjusted treatment failures at day 28 in the atovaquone-proguanil group (9.4%) compared to two in the artesunate-amodiaquine group (2.9%). The risk ratio (RR) was 3.19 (95% CI 0.67 to 15.22), based on low-certainty evidence. PCR-unadjusted treatment failures were similar between the groups, with 14.1% in the atovaquone-proguanil group and 11.8% in the artesunate-amodiaquine group (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.49 to 2.91; low-certainty evidence). 3. Comparison with Artesunate-Mefloquine: A 2012 trial in Colombia and a 2002 trial in Thailand (a region with high levels of multi-drug-resistant malaria) showed similar PCR-adjusted treatment failure rates at day 42: 2.7% in the atovaquone-proguanil group versus 2.4% in the artesunate-mefloquine group (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.57 to 2.34; high-certainty evidence). PCR-unadjusted treatment failures were also comparable, with 5.3% in the atovaquone-proguanil group and 6.6% in the artesunate-mefloquine group (RR 0.8, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.3; low-certainty evidence). 4. Combination of Atovaquone-Proguanil with Artesunate: When atovaquone-proguanil was combined with artesunate, there were fewer treatment failures at day 28 and day 42, both with and without PCR adjustment. At day 28, PCR-adjusted treatment failures were 2.16% in the atovaquone-proguanil group compared to no failures in the artesunate-atovaquone-proguanil group (RR 5.14, 95% CI 0.61 to 43.52; low-certainty evidence). At day 42, PCR-adjusted treatment failures were 3.82% in the atovaquone-proguanil group compared to 2.05% in the artesunate-atovaquone-proguanil group (RR 1.84, 95% CI 0.95 to 3.56; moderate-certainty evidence). In the 2002 trial in Thailand, the artesunate-atovaquone-proguanil group had fewer treatment failures at day 42 compared to the atovaquone-proguanil group. Adverse events were reported across the trials, but no consistent patterns emerged to suggest that atovaquone-proguanil is strongly associated with any specific adverse event. In conclusion, atovaquone-proguanil is effective for treating uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, although treatment failure rates ranged between 5% and 10% in some cases. The addition of artesunate to atovaquone-proguanil may reduce treatment failure rates. Further research is warranted to explore the combination of artesunate-atovaquone-proguanil and the potential development of parasite resistance.
